How I got here

I grew up near Mannheim in southwest Germany and studied business in Heidelberg, with a focus on marketing and sales. Somewhere along the way I noticed that the part of the work I enjoyed most was rarely the pitch. It was the spreadsheet behind it.

That became clear at 11teamsports. Two of us ran the company’s marketplace business, selling surplus stock on Amazon, Zalando and About You, worth around €15,000 to €20,000 a day. Every morning started with the numbers, and more than once they told us something was wrong before any customer did. I’ve wanted to work that way ever since.

So in 2025 I moved to Boston for a Master in Management with a concentration in Business Analytics, and stayed for a Master of Finance. One taught me how to work with data, the other what to ask of it. Outside class, I look after the budget of the Hult Student Association as Treasurer and represent my cohort as class representative.

I do my best work where things move quickly, the work is digital and you can see what your analysis changed. That’s what I’m looking for next.

Things I’ve built

Eight projects from my two master’s programs, from a real client engagement to SQL portfolio analytics and machine learning. Open one to see the question behind it, how I approached it, what came out, and where available the slides, dashboards and code.

The setup: a high-net-worth client with roughly $95 million spread across five ETFs wants to know whether the portfolio is still built the right way. The constraint for this assignment was that every number had to come out of the database itself, with no spreadsheet in between.

The question

How have IXN (global technology), QQQ (Nasdaq-100), IEF (7 to 10 year Treasuries), VNQ (US real estate) and GLD (gold) performed over 12, 18 and 24 months, how much risk does each position add, and what should the client sell or buy?

What I did

I loaded three years of daily prices into MySQL and wrote stored procedures that calculate the return over each window, the monthly variance and the annualized sigma, so every figure can be rerun with a single call. Looking at the holdings side by side showed that IXN and QQQ largely own the same large tech names, so the client was paying twice for one bet. I then passed new weights into the same procedures to compare the current and the proposed portfolio on identical terms.

The result

Sell 10% of IEF and 5% of QQQ and move that 15% into DBC, a broad commodity ETF that behaves differently from both tech stocks and bonds. On 12-month data, the expected portfolio return rises from 38.74% to 43.19% while annualized sigma falls from 12.25% to 11.77%. More return for less risk is rare, and it came from removing an overlap rather than taking a bigger bet.

This was a real client project. The Revolution’s question sounds simple: Boston hosts World Cup matches at the club’s own stadium, and hundreds of thousands of soccer fans will be in town. How does a Major League Soccer club make sure that excitement doesn’t leave with them? Our final deck had 31 slides and covered everything from the diagnosis to a roadmap.

The question

Where does the club lose fans today, which groups in Boston are most likely to stick, and what has to happen in June and July 2026 so that a World Cup visitor ends up with a Revolution ticket?

What we did

We analyzed fan feedback with NLP, sized the most promising audiences, and designed a capture-and-convert funnel around the club app, with concrete tactics, timing and a prototype. Details below.

The result

A four-pillar strategy: fix the digital ticket funnel first, capture three target segments at the Fan Zone and on campuses, convert them with a student Rev-Pass and a $5 first match, and add a B2B channel for companies and universities.

What we found before we touched the World Cup

We started with what fans actually say. Running NLP on 412 fan documents (app store reviews, ticketing feedback, social posts and forum threads from 2025 and 2026), we saw that interest was not the problem. 54.7% of fan conversation was about digital friction, sentiment about Ticketmaster was 77.8% negative, and 50.6% of app users showed signs of churn. Only 0.2% of the documents connected the club to the World Cup at all. Our headline for the client: the problem is the pipeline, not the product.

  • 54.7%of fan conversation is about digital friction
  • 77.8%of Ticketmaster sentiment is negative
  • 50.6%of app users show churn signals
  • 0.2%of fan documents mention the World Cup

Who we went after

Instead of “everyone who watches a World Cup game”, we sized three segments that are already in Boston and already care about soccer: the Hispanic community (about 131,000 people in Boston, 44% of whom follow World Cup 2026), international students (about 84,000 in Massachusetts) and young adults aged 18 to 39 (about 354,000). Each one gets its own way in.

The plan: four pillars

  1. Fix the pipeline. Remove forced account creation, take the friction out of ticketing and get to a one-tap ticket purchase. Without this, every other idea leaks.
  2. Activate the three segments with a mix of physical and digital capture, so no paid media is needed to get the first contact.
  3. Convert with a Rev-Pass. A $25 a month student bundle with public transit included, a semester commitment and sign-up only through the app.
  4. Open the B2B channel. Group deals for hospitals, pharma companies, universities and student governments around Boston.

How it works on the ground

The club app is the conversion goal because it is the only channel the club owns: first-party data, push notifications and a direct path to a ticket. To get people into it, we proposed QR wristbands at the FIFA Fan Zone on City Hall Plaza (16 days) and campus pop-ups: one scan means an app download and an entry into a raffle for a VIP match experience. Visitors who opt in can be reached again two to three days later with Revolution ads on Instagram and TikTok through location-based retargeting. During the tournament, a weekly World Cup prediction game keeps them opening the app, with points that turn into ticket discounts. Within 48 hours of the final, a “Your first match for $5” push turns the emotional high into a first visit, and a referral link lets every new fan bring friends. The goal in one sentence: a student who downloads the app in June 2026 is a season ticket holder by 2027.

Tools we used

Minto pyramid and SCQA to build the storyline, an issue tree to split the problem, NLP sentiment analysis, segment sizing from public data, Porter’s five forces, SWOT and Ansoff, a 2×2 prioritization of tactics and a four-phase roadmap up to 2030. To show the idea is buildable, we also prototyped a World Cup Hub as a small working web app.

Semester at Sea runs university voyages around the world, and students pay their tuition in installments. Ahead of a board meeting, leadership wanted one page that answers where the money stands. I worked from the raw tables for bookings, invoices and payments, and the page had to be readable in two minutes by people who will never open Power BI themselves.

The question

How much revenue has been invoiced and recognized, how much is still outstanding, which students and voyage terms drive revenue, and where does the payment process create risk?

What I did

I built the data model in Power BI and wrote DAX measures for invoiced, collected and outstanding revenue. Revenue is recognized by voyage term, so it shows up in the period the voyage actually happens, and a waterfall walks from contracted revenue down to what is still open. While building it I documented the data quality issues I ran into, for example installments without a due date, which make it impossible to say what is actually overdue.

The result

$37.46M invoiced, an 84.8% collection rate and $5.70M still outstanding. Students who sail more than one term bring in 3.6 times the revenue per person, so I recommended a loyalty offer for returning students and automatic payment reminders, and I listed the missing due dates as the first data fix before the next board cycle.

For this assignment I picked a business I know from the inside: the marketplace resale unit at 11teamsports, where I worked in 2025. It sells leftover teamwear, boots and training wear on Amazon, Zalando and About You. I built a ten-sheet Excel model, from assumptions and cost structure to a monthly budget, for a FY2027 plan of €4.75M in net revenue.

The question

How resilient is the unit if sales fall, how far can it discount before a sale stops making sense, and is a €18,000 AI tool that automates listings, category mapping and price syncing worth the money?

What I did

I separated variable from fixed costs, using the high-low method to split the warehouse as a mixed cost, and treated the book value of the overstock as sunk. That changes the picture: 95.8% of costs are variable, so the unit covers its annual fixed costs after about 75 sales days. From there I calculated a weighted contribution margin across jerseys, boots and training wear, a price floor per product line, a stress test for higher return rates and a three-year NPV for the automation tool.

The result

Break-even sits at about 33,000 units, with a 79% margin of safety. The tool saves half a full-time role and has an NPV of about €10,500 at a 13.8% discount rate, so I recommended buying it. The most useful finding came from the scenarios: losing 20% of volume cuts operating income by a quarter, but the same revenue drop through deeper discounts wipes out almost the entire margin and pushes the unit into a loss. The rule for the team: protect the price floor.

The client in this project is modeled on Ken Fisher: three accounts holding Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia, JPMorgan and the IEF Treasury ETF, worth about $85 billion at the latest prices. I set up the database myself, with customer, account, holdings and security tables plus three years of daily prices (June 2023 to June 2026) for every ticker and for VOO as the S&P 500 benchmark.

The question

How much return does each position deliver for the risk it adds, how sensitive is the whole portfolio to the market, and is there one change that improves the risk-adjusted return?

What I did

I calculated daily returns with window functions (LAG over each ticker), scaled them to monthly return and risk, and ranked every holding by its Sharpe ratio with a 4.5% risk-free rate. Beta against VOO comes straight from covariance and variance in SQL. Then I tested adding Newmont (NEM), a gold miner with a below-market beta, stored the new allocation in its own table and compared the current and the optimized portfolio in one query.

The result

Nvidia, JPMorgan and Alphabet earn the most per unit of risk, while Microsoft and the Treasury ETF barely beat, or fall short of, the risk-free rate in this period. Shifting weight toward Alphabet, JPMorgan and Nvidia, trimming Apple and Microsoft and adding 7% Newmont lifts the expected monthly return from 2.47% to 2.98% and the Sharpe ratio from 0.26 to 0.30. The trade-off is a slightly higher beta, 1.17 to 1.21, which is a decision the client has to make consciously.

# daily adjusted prices and returns, checking code works
SELECT z.*,(z.P1-z.P0)/z.P0 as ROR
FROM(
SELECT ticker,date, adj_close AS P1, LAG(adj_close,1)OVER(
                                              PARTITION BY ticker
                                              ORDER BY date) 
                                              as P0
FROM SMART_investments.pricing_daily_new
)z;

# monthly return & risk(standard deviation) per ticker
SELECT s.ticker, s.expected_ror * 21 as monthly_return, s.risk * sqrt(21) as monthly_risk
FROM(
SELECT y.ticker, avg(y.ROR) as expected_ror, std(y.ROR) as risk
FROM(
SELECT z.*, (z.P1-z.P0)/z.P0 as ROR
FROM(
SELECT ticker, date, adj_close as P1, LAG(adj_close,1) OVER (
                                               PARTITION BY ticker 
                                               ORDER BY date) 
                                               as P0
FROM SMART_investments.pricing_daily_new
WHERE ticker in ('AAPL','AMZN','MSFT','GOOGL','NVDA','JPM','IEF')
) z
) y
GROUP BY y.ticker
) s
ORDER BY monthly_return DESC;

# sharpe ratio per ticker
SELECT y.ticker, avg(y.ROR) / std(y.ROR) as sharpe_ratio
FROM(
SELECT z.ticker, (z.P1 - z.P0)/ z.P0 as ROR
FROM(
SELECT ticker, date, adj_close as P1, LAG(adj_close, 1) OVER(
                                               PARTITION BY ticker 
                                               ORDER BY date) 
                                               as P0
FROM SMART_investments.pricing_daily_new
)z
) y
GROUP BY y.ticker
ORDER BY sharpe_ratio DESC;

# monthly sharpe ratio (with risk free rate 4.50%) & beta per ticker
SELECT s.ticker,(avg(s.ROR) - 0.045/252) * 21/(std(s.ROR) * sqrt(21)) as sharpe_ratio,(avg(s.ROR * m.market_ROR) - avg(s.ROR) * avg(m.market_ROR))/(avg(m.market_ROR * m.market_ROR) - avg(m.market_ROR) * avg(m.market_ROR)) as beta
FROM(
SELECT z.ticker, z.date, (z.P1 - z.P0)/ z.P0 as ROR
FROM(
SELECT ticker, date, adj_close as P1, LAG(adj_close, 1) OVER(
                                               PARTITION BY ticker 
                                               ORDER BY date) 
                                               as P0
FROM SMART_investments.pricing_daily_new
WHERE ticker IN ('AAPL','AMZN','MSFT','GOOGL','NVDA','JPM','IEF')
) z
) s
JOIN(
SELECT z.date, (z.P1 - z.P0)/ z.P0 as market_ROR
FROM(
SELECT date, adj_close as P1,LAG(adj_close, 1) 
                                      OVER (ORDER BY date) 
                                      as P0
FROM SMART_investments.pricing_daily_new
WHERE ticker = 'VOO'
) z
) m ON s.date = m.date
GROUP BY s.ticker
ORDER BY sharpe_ratio DESC
;

# current holdings of potfolio
SELECT h.ticker, (h.quantity * p.P1) / z.price as current_weight
FROM holdings_dim as h
JOIN(
SELECT ticker, adj_close as P1
FROM pricing_daily_new
WHERE (ticker, date) in (SELECT ticker, max(date) FROM pricing_daily_new GROUP BY ticker)

CROSS JOIN(

FROM holdings_dim as h2

SELECT ticker, adj_close as P1
FROM pricing_daily_new
WHERE (ticker, date) in (SELECT ticker, MAX(date) FROM pricing_daily_new GROUP BY ticker)
) p2 on h2.ticker = p2.ticker
) z
;

# return & risk(standard deviation) ADDING NEM

FROM(

FROM(

FROM optimized_weights as o
JOIN(

FROM pricing_daily_new

GROUP BY y.ticker
) s on o.ticker = s.ticker

SELECT c.ticker,(avg(c.ROR*m.market_ROR) -avg(c.ROR)*avg(m.market_ROR))/(avg(m.market_ROR*m.market_ROR)- avg(m.market_ROR)*avg(m.market_ROR)) as beta
FROM(
SELECT z.ticker, z.date,(z.P1-z.P0)/z.P0 as ROR
FROM (SELECT ticker, date, adj_close as P1,LAG(adj_close,1) OVER (

                                                    as P0
FROM pricing_daily_new) z
) c

An industrial dataset with sensor readings for 10,000 machines: air and process temperature, rotational speed, torque and tool wear. Only 339 of them failed. That is exactly what makes the problem hard: a model that always says “no failure” is already 96.6% accurate and completely useless.

The question

Can we predict which machine fails next early enough for maintenance to step in, and which signals give a failure away?

What I did

I split the data with stratification so training and test sets keep the same 3.39% failure rate, then trained four models: a scaled logistic regression as the baseline, a decision tree tuned over depths 1 to 15, a random forest tuned with grid search and class weights, and XGBoost with extra weight on the rare class. I judged them on precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC instead of accuracy, because a missed failure and a technician sent out for nothing have very different costs.

The result

The tuned decision tree (max depth 10) gave the best balance: it catches 77% of all failures and 79% of its alarms are real, compared with 14% recall for the baseline. XGBoost and the random forest rank machines slightly better overall, but raise more false alarms. I recommended the tree, because a maintenance team can follow every rule it uses, with torque, tool wear and rotational speed as the strongest signals.

Decision tree, max depth 10 (recommended)0.790.770.780.90

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = df.drop(columns=['Type', 'Machine failure'])
y = df['Machine failure']

# stratify=y keeps the same ~3.4% failure rate in both train and test sets -
# without this, a random split could leave the test set with very few
# (or even zero) failures to evaluate against
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

print('Train failures:', y_train.sum(), '/', len(y_train))
print('Test failures:', y_test.sum(), '/', len(y_test))

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# Logistic Regression is sensitive to feature scale (unlike trees), so we
# standardize first. We fit the scaler on the training set only and apply
# it to the test set, to avoid leaking test-set information into training
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

logreg = LogisticRegression(random_state=42, max_iter=1000)
logreg.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
    roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix
)

def evaluate(y_true, y_pred, y_proba, label):
    print(f'--- {label} ---')
    print('Accuracy: ', round(accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred), 3))
    print('Precision:', round(precision_score(y_true, y_pred), 3))
    print('Recall:   ', round(recall_score(y_true, y_pred), 3))
    print('F1:       ', round(f1_score(y_true, y_pred), 3))
    print('ROC-AUC:  ', round(roc_auc_score(y_true, y_proba), 3))
    print('Confusion matrix:')
    print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
    return {'model': label, 'accuracy': accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
            'precision': precision_score(y_true, y_pred), 'recall': recall_score(y_true, y_pred),
            'f1': f1_score(y_true, y_pred), 'roc_auc': roc_auc_score(y_true, y_proba)}

results = []

y_pred_lr = logreg.predict(X_test_scaled)
y_proba_lr = logreg.predict_proba(X_test_scaled)[:, 1]
results.append(evaluate(y_test, y_pred_lr, y_proba_lr, 'Logistic Regression (baseline)'))

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

# Unrestricted decision tree - no depth limit, so it grows until every leaf
# is pure. Comparing train vs. test performance tells us whether the model
# is learning generalizable patterns or just memorizing the training data.
dtc = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)
dtc.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_train = dtc.predict(X_train)
y_pred_test = dtc.predict(X_test)

print('Train F1:', round(f1_score(y_train, y_pred_train), 3))
print('Test F1: ', round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_test), 3))
print('Tree depth:', dtc.get_depth())

#searching for the perfect tree depth at where the improvement is not huge anymore or even is controproductive
f1_train_list = []
f1_test_list = []
depths = range(1, 16)

for depth in depths:
    dtr = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=42)
    dtr.fit(X_train, y_train)
    f1_train_list.append(f1_score(y_train, dtr.predict(X_train)))
    f1_test_list.append(f1_score(y_test, dtr.predict(X_test)))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.plot(depths, f1_train_list, label='train F1')
plt.plot(depths, f1_test_list, label='test F1')
plt.legend(loc='best')
plt.xlabel('max_depth')
plt.ylabel('F1 score')
plt.title('Decision Tree: F1 vs. max_depth')
plt.show()

best_depth = depths[f1_test_list.index(max(f1_test_list))]
print('Best max_depth by test F1:', best_depth)

# Refit a Decision Tree using the best depth found above, and evaluate it
# properly (this is the version that goes into our final comparison table)
dtc_best = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=best_depth, random_state=42)
dtc_best.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_dt = dtc_best.predict(X_test)
y_proba_dt = dtc_best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

results.append(evaluate(y_test, y_pred_dt, y_proba_dt, f'Decision Tree (max_depth={best_depth})'))

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Random Forest: ensemble of many trees trained on random subsets of rows
# and features, then averaged - this reduces the variance problem we saw
# with the single Decision Tree. class_weight='balanced' pushes the model
# to pay more attention to the rare failure class, and GridSearchCV tunes
# the remaining hyperparameters, scored on F1 (not accuracy).
param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200],
    'max_depth': [5, 10, None],
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 5],
}

rf = RandomForestClassifier(class_weight='balanced', random_state=42)

grid_search = GridSearchCV(rf, param_grid, scoring='f1', cv=3, n_jobs=-1)
grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print('Best params:', grid_search.best_params_)
best_rf = grid_search.best_estimator_

y_pred_rf = best_rf.predict(X_test)
y_proba_rf = best_rf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

results.append(evaluate(y_test, y_pred_rf, y_proba_rf, 'Random Forest (tuned, class-weighted)'))

import xgboost as xgb

# scale_pos_weight rebalances the loss similarly to class_weight='balanced' -
# it's the ratio of majority to minority class in the training set
scale_pos_weight = (y_train == 0).sum() / (y_train == 1).sum()

xgb_clf = xgb.XGBClassifier(random_state=42, scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight, eval_metric='logloss')
xgb_clf.fit(X_train.values, y_train.values)  # .values avoids a column-name issue with brackets like '[K]'

y_pred_xgb = xgb_clf.predict(X_test.values)
y_proba_xgb = xgb_clf.predict_proba(X_test.values)[:, 1]

results.append(evaluate(y_test, y_pred_xgb, y_proba_xgb, 'XGBoost (scale_pos_weight)'))

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).set_index('model')
print(results_df.round(3))

results_df[['precision', 'recall', 'f1', 'roc_auc']].plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10, 5))
plt.title('Model comparison')
plt.ylabel('Score')
plt.xticks(rotation=15)
plt.legend(loc='lower right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

A retailer sells books, computers, home and kitchen products, mobile devices and video games across Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America and Oceania. Management asked two direct questions, and we answered them with a Power BI report and a short memo.

The question

Which country manager really performs best, and does it make sense to discontinue the book line?

What we did

We built pages for revenue trends by product line, a sales map by country, manager cards and two decision pages. For the managers we looked beyond total revenue to revenue per sale and a performance ratio, and added GNI per capita as economic context for each country. For books we compared the three-year CAGR of every product line and region.

The result

Emma Smith (USA) leads with $211.9M in revenue and is also among the most efficient per sale. Australia grew fastest, by 37% from 2017 to 2018, while wealthy markets like Belgium and France are stagnating. Books fell 28% over three years while home and kitchen, video games and mobile each grew more than 20%, but the decline is much milder in Oceania and Latin America. Our advice: don’t cut books yet. First bring product margins, inventory costs and cross-selling data into the pipeline, because revenue alone can’t answer that question.

A bike-sharing service shared one quarter of hourly rental data, with temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation and rain for every hour. Rentals drop in late autumn, and the business wanted to know who its remaining customers are so it can serve them better.

The question

What motivates most customers to rent a bike in late autumn and winter, and how much does the weather really matter?

What I did

I cleaned and typed the data in pandas, turned the holiday and functioning-day flags into numbers and extracted hour, month and weekday from the timestamp. Then I ran a Pearson correlation of rentals against every variable, drew a heatmap, plotted average demand by hour of day and fitted regression plots for the two strongest weather drivers, temperature and solar radiation.

The result

Demand peaks around 8am and 6pm on working days, so the typical winter customer is a commuter, not a leisure rider. Warmer and sunnier hours do lift rentals, but the time of day explains more than the weather. My recommendations were built around commuters, such as making sure bikes are available at stations during rush hour.

#INSERT OF THE RELEVANT DATASET AND PACKAGES
#before we can insert the file itself we have to insert packages to answer the questions
#we need pandas to work with data science tools
import pandas as pd
#we need matplotlib.pyplot to create visualizations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
#we need seaborn for advanced visualizations
import seaborn as sns

#to suppress all user warnings and future warnings
import warnings
warnings.simplefilter(action= "ignore",category= UserWarning)
#suppress all warnings from pandas or seaborn
warnings.simplefilter(action = 'ignore', category = FutureWarning)

#storing the path to the dataset, if we would store it locally then the user using the script wont see the file
file = "bikes_data.xlsx"

#converting holiday and functioning day with a dictionary to read the file later with describe()
data_types = {"Holiday":str,
             "FunctioningDay": str}

#to read the file in Python with the help of pandas
bikedata = pd.read_excel(io = file,
                        sheet_name = "data",
                        header = 0,
                        dtype = data_types)

#display the first 5 rows to check if the code is working
bikedata.head(n=5)


#CHECK IF EVERY COLUMN IS INCLUDED
#analyzing if every column of the excelsheet is included and also what kind of datatype it is
bikedata.info(verbose = True)


#Analysis of the statistics for numeric values
#describe shows all the statistics for the numeric data. Also it is rounded on 2 decimals
#unfortunaly Holdiday and Functioning day cant be shown since they are no numbers in the excel sheet
bikedata.describe(include = 'number').round(decimals = 2)


#Analysis of the statistics for non numeric values
#describe shows all the statistics with include we can also show the non numeric values
#since we analyzed before the numeric values we now have a look on the objects
bikedata.describe(include = 'object')


#convertion of Holiday and FunctioningDay to numbers (changing from yes/no to 0/1)
#this helps us later to calculate the correlation with those variables included since they are als important for the renting behavior
#Code was created with the help of AI, the prompt iss linked in the appendix
#Prompt 2 was used to help with the code

#with the '=' we told Python to rewrite the normal Holiday with the new formula
#map means rewriting of the part so every 1 gets changed to a Yes and every No to a 0
bikedata['Holiday'] = bikedata['Holiday'].map({'Yes':1,'No':0})

#with the '=' we told Python to rewrite the normal FunctioningDay with the new formula
#map means rewriting of the part so every 1 gets changed to a Yes and every No to a 0
bikedata['FunctioningDay'] = bikedata['FunctioningDay'].map({'Yes':1,'No':0})


#Extracting of hour, month and weekday
#extracting the hour and month from the DateHour column which helps to analyze the customer behavior
#dt.hour extracts the hour from the datetime column and creates a new one with the '='
bikedata['Hour'] = bikedata['DateHour'].dt.hour

#dt.month extracts the hour from the datetime column and creates a new one with the '='
bikedata['Month']= bikedata['DateHour'].dt.month

#dt.dayofweek extracts the hour from the datetime column and creates a new one with the '='
bikedata['Weekday'] = bikedata['DateHour'].dt.dayofweek 


#calculation of the correlation between the rentals and all the variables which could have an impact on the rental behavoir
#this helps to find the best correlation to show then as a scatterplot in the following. 
#the correlation was built with the formula used in class with the pearson method and 2 decimals.
#since I got a error here I used AI which then explained that we need to only include numeric values to make it work
# the AI promt is linked below in the references
#promt 1 was used here
bikes_corr = bikedata.select_dtypes(include = 'number').corr(method = "pearson").round(decimals =2)

#specification of the plotsize with a 12 by 12 size
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize = (12,12))

# Input inspired from lecture slides 8, each of the rows determines a part of the heatmap
sns.heatmap(data = bikes_corr, #dataset used for the heatmap
           cmap = 'inferno', #colorset used to make the colors stand out
           square = True,  #to make the layout square
           annot = True, # to include the numbers itself to the scatterplot so the user can visually see them
           linecolor = 'black', # linecolor got changed to black
           linewidths = 0.5) #thickness of the lines got changed

#adding of a title with plt.title
plt.title(label = """
Linear Correlation Heatmap between Bike Rental Reasons""")

# showing the visualization
plt.show(block = True)


#Linechart for Hour and Rentals

#specifying of the plot size; figsize sets the width and height of the plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize = (12,8))

#the formula for a lineplot was created with the help of AI since i didnt know the term sns.lineplot

Average Bike Rentals by Hour of Day
         """)

#showing the visualization with plt.show
#block = True tells the code to show the visual before continuing

#Scatterplot of the relation between Rental Demand and Temperature
#creation of a scatterflot for the variable with the highest corralation: temperature

#scatterplot of temperature vs rentals with the code used in session 8
sns.lmplot(data = bikedata,
